abstract: Sustainable production of plant secondary metabolites remains a substantial challenge. Microbial cell factories offer a promising solution, yet reconstituting plant cytochrome P450s, key enzymes in these pathways, remains a major hurdle. In this study, we investigated a plant membrane protein, AtMSBP1, for its ability to broadly enhance P450 functionality in engineered yeast. Unlike in plants, interactions with cytochrome P450s are not essential for AtMSBP1’s function in yeast. Specifically, AtMSBP1 orchestrates interorganelle communication, involving not only the endoplasmic reticulum but also mitochondria and vacuoles, supporting cytochrome P450s functionality in yeast. This study highlights the critical role of cross-organelle coordination in supporting cytochrome P450s functionality, emphasizing a shift from traditional ER-based approaches to engineering cross-organelle interactions and tailoring the cellular microenvironment to enhance plant cytochrome P450s functionality in yeast.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
General culture conditions
Yeast strains were cultured in 30°C in a complex yeast extract, peptone, and dextrose (YPD; all components from BD Diagnostics) medium or synthetic defined medium (SDM) containing yeast nitrogen base (YNB) (BD Diagnostics), ammonium sulfate (Fisher Scientific), 2% (w/v) glucose, unless specified, and the appropriate dropout (Takara Bio) solution for selection.
For metabolite analysis, yeast strains were first cultured overnight in 500 μl of SDM with 2% (w/v) glucose in 96-well plates (BD Falcon) at 30°C overnight, at 250 rpm. The appropriate volume of the overnight seed culture was inoculated in fresh 500-μl SDM with glucose to make the OD
600
around 0.1 and incubated at 30°C for 72 hours before metabolite analysis of the yeast pellets or medium. The OD
600
of the culture was measured by a Molecular Devices QuickDrop Spectrophotometer.
General technique for DNA manipulation
PCR reactions were performed with an Expand High Fidelity system (Sigma-Aldrich), Phusion DNA Polymerase (NEB), Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (New England Biolabs), or Taq Polymerase (NEB) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. PCR products were purified by the Zymoclean Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research). Plasmids were prepared with EconoSpin columns (Epoch Life Science) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. All DNA constructs were confirmed through DNA sequencing by the Azenta Life Science Inc. BP Clonase II Enzyme Mix, Gateway pDONR221 Vector, and LR Clonase II Enzyme Mix (Life Technologies), and the
S. cerevisiae
Advanced Gateway Destination Vector Kit (Addgene) was used to perform the gateway cloning. The Gibson one-pot, isothermal DNA assembly (
59
) was conducted at the scale of 10 μl by incubating T5 exonuclease (NEB), Phusion polymerase (NEB), Taq ligase (NEB), and 50 ng of each DNA fragment at 50°C for 1 hour to assemble multiple DNA fragments. Yeast strains are constructed through homologous recombination and DNA assembly (
60
). Yeast strains and plasmids and amino acid sequences of genes used in this work are listed in data S1 and table S2, respectively.
Analysis and quantification of 22-OH-4-en-3-one
22-OH-4-en-3-one was extracted and analyzed from yeast pellets. To extract free sterols from yeast, 100 μl of acetone was added to yeast cell pellets (from 500-μl yeast culture), followed by the addition of 400 μl of methanol with vigorous vortex to mix. The supernatant was transferred to new tubes. The extraction of the pellets was repeated by an additional 400-μl ethyl acetate. The supernatants were combined and dried in the vacufuge (Eppendorf). The dried samples were dissolved in 40 μl of methanol.
The samples were then analyzed by reversed-phase liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC-MS) on a Shimadzu 2020 single quadrupole LC-MS (Poroshell 120, EC-C18, 3.0 mm by 100 mm, 2.7 μm) using positive ionization. To analyze sterols, the metabolites were separated under the linear gradient started from 80% methanol (v/v in water and 0.1% formic acid) to 100% methanol (v/v in water and 0.1% formic acid) for 8 min followed by 100% methanol (v/v in water and 0.1% formic acid) for 12 min at a flow rate of 0.5 ml/min. Data were acquired through the electrospray ionization mode. The sterols were analyzed using selected ion monitoring (SIM) with either the characteristic or possible mass/charge ratio (
m/z
+
) according to the structures and molecular weights.

The yeast culture was centrifuged, and the supernatant was then analyzed by reversed-phase LC-MS on a Shimadzu 2020 single quadrupole LC-MS (Poroshell 120, EC-C18, 3.0 mm by 100 mm, 2.7 μm) using positive ionization. GPD

Yeast cells were subsequently harvested and lysed with 300 μl of protein extraction buffer [100 mM NaCl, 20 mM Hepes-NaOH at pH 7.4, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), and protease inhibitor] and 100 μl of 0.5-mm glass beads. The mixture was vortexed vigorously three times for 40 s, where the samples were kept on ice between each vortex. The supernatant of the cell lysate was collected, and 300 μl of membrane protein extraction buffer [100 mM NaCl, 20 mM Hepes-NaOH at pH 7.4, 20% (w/v) glycerol, and 2% Triton X-100] was added to the cell lysate pellet to resuspend it. The suspension was incubated with rotation at 4°C for 1 hour to completely dissolve the membrane proteins. The supernatant was collected and combined with the first-round supernatant. To the solution was subsequently added 20 μl of anti-GFP magnetic beads (MBL-D153-11 from MBL). After incubation with rotation at 4°C overnight, the beads were washed four times with phosphate-buffered saline buffer (137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 10 mM Na

4
) and then resuspended in 40 μl of 1× loading buffer and incubated at 95°C for 10 min. Five microliters of the samples was used for Western blot analysis to confirm the expression of AtMSBP1-EGFP and EGFP. The remaining samples were subjected to in-gel tryptic digestion following a previously described protocol (
61
,
62
). In brief, gel bands corresponding to proteins with a molecular weight greater than 15 kDa were excised and cut into ~1-mm
3
pieces. The gel fragments were sequentially destained using 25 and 50% acetonitrile in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (pH 7.8). Cysteine residues in proteins were reduced with 10 mM DTT at 37°C for 1 hour and subsequently alkylated with 55 mM iodoacetamide at room temperature (RT) in the dark for 20 min. Proteins were then digested in-gel with trypsin at an enzyme-to-protein ratio of 1:50 (w/w) in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (pH 7.8) at 37°C for 16 hours. Peptides were extracted from the gel pieces by sequential shaking in 25 and 50% acetonitrile containing 5% acetic acid. The resulting tryptic peptides were desalted using C18 ZipTip (Pierce) and dried by a SpeedVac. The tandem mass tag (TMT; 126 to 131, Thermo Fisher Scientific) labeling experiment was performed following a previously described protocol (
63
). Briefly, the desalted peptides were reconstituted in 8.5 μl of 50 mM Hepes (pH 8.5) and 1.5 μl of TMT reagents was added from stocks dissolved in 100% anhydrous acetonitrile. The peptide-TMT mixture was incubated via vortex at RT for 2 hours. The labeling reaction was terminated by addition of 0.9 μl of quenching solution (5% hydroxylamine in 50 mM Hepes (pH 8.5)] and vortexing at RT for 15 min. The labeled samples were mixed with 8.92 μl of 10% formic acid/10% acetonitrile. All the samples were pooled, dried by vacuum centrifugation, desalted, and subjected to liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis.
LC-MS and MS/MS analyses were conducted on a Fusion Lumos Orbitrap tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with an Easy 1000 nLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a Flex nanoelectrospray ion source (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The mass spectrometer was equipped with a high-field asymmetric-waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS), where the compensation voltages (CVs) were set at −40, −60, and −80 V. The carrier gas flow was set at 4.2 liters/min. The cycle time was 3 s with each CV being scanned for 1 s. The LC conditions were the same as those described for LC-MRM analysis except that a 160-min linear gradient of 12 to 34% buffer B was used. The spray voltage was set as 2 kV, and the ion transfer tube temperature was 320°C. The mass spectrometer was operated in the data-dependent acquisition mode, where MS was acquired with Orbitrap at a resolution of 50,000. Fragmentation was conducted with higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) at a relative collisional energy of 38. The MS/MS were acquired in the Orbitrap.
The raw LC-MS/MS data were processed using MaxQuant version 1.6.15.0 software. Both MS and MS/MS mass tolerances were set at 20 ppm (parts per million). Fixed modification was applied for cysteine carbamidomethylation, whereas variable modifications included methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. Peptides were filtered on the basis of a 1% false discovery rate (FDR), allowing a maximum of two trypsin missed cleavages. Replicate samples were aligned within a time window of 0.7 min. Protein identification was performed by searching for the mass spectra against a Yeast UniProt database (UP000002311) modified by adding seven protein sequences (i.e., DWF1, DWF5, DWF7, CYP90A1, CYP90B1, ATR1, and AtMSBP1) from
Arabidopsis
as well as GFP, using a target-decoy approach. The identified proteins were filtered at a 1% protein FDR. For protein quantification, intensities for reporter ions (MS
2
) were used.
The mbSUS-Y2H system to detect protein-protein interaction
For the Y2H assay, we followed a standard protocol for the mbSUS-Y2H system. Briefly, the encoding genes of proteins to be detected were cloned to pDonor221 (Invitrogen) without stop codons. Those genes were then used with Gateway LR Clonase II to clone into the pMetYC-DEST vector to generate the bait constructs with Cub fused to the C termini of encoding genes or into the pXN22-DEST vector to generate prey constructs with Nub fused to the C termini of encoding genes (data S1). The bait and prey constructs were transformed into CD3-808 and CD3-809 yeast strains and selected on –Leu and –Trp/–Ura plates, respectively. By mating, the diploid cells harboring both constructs were selected on –Trp, –Leu, and –Ura plates. Positive cells were serially diluted and plated on the six selective medium –Trp, –Leu, –Ade, –His, –Ura, and –Met. Images were taken after 3 to 5 days of growth. In the mbSUS-Y2H system, bait and prey proteins are separately fused with N terminus (Nub) and C terminus (Cub) of a ubiquitin. Because MAPR proteins, AtCYP90B1 and RTN1, VMA2 fused with Cub always result in background growth, we can only test the interactions of MAPR-Nub with AtCYP90A1-Cub and PsCYP82Y1-Cub. The interaction between AtMSBP1 and RTN1, VMA2, was validated through BiFC.

Confocal microscopy imaging
All the images were taken in live cells. Cell culture was cultivated in SDM as described in the “General culture conditions” section. After cultivation, 5 μl of the cell suspension in the SDM was loaded on 1 inch–by–3 inch glass slides and covered with 22 mm–by–22 mm coverslips. Fresh samples were made for each imaging. The confocal images were obtained by fluorescence laser-scan confocal microscopy Nikon AXR. The laser was set to 488 nm to excite EGFP fluorescence. Organelles were labeled by different proteins. Mitochondria: COX15-EGFP was expressed downstream of the
GPD

INTRODUCTION
Plant secondary metabolites hold indispensable pharmaceutical and agricultural value, yet sourcing them has always been challenging (
1
,
2
). Now, almost all plant secondary metabolites are obtained through direct extraction from plant materials (
3
). Microbial production has emerged as a promising alternative (
4
,
5
); however, reconstituting the function of plant enzymes remains a major hurdle in these engineering efforts (
6
). Among all plant enzyme types, efficiently reconstituting plant cytochrome P450 (CYP) functions has been particularly important yet challenging. CYPs are major players in metabolism across all kingdoms, including secondary metabolic pathways in plants. As of 2018, more than 32,000 plant CYPs have been identified, with the number rapidly increasing as more genomes become available (
7
). Such prevalence of CYPs reflects their essential roles in contributing to the structural diversity of plant metabolites. Notably, plant CYPs are predominantly type II CYPs localized at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane and require a redox partner, generally referred as cytochrome P450 reductase (CPR), for catalysis (
8
). This poses additional challenges for the functional reconstitution of these membrane-bound proteins in microbial hosts (
8
).
Despite numerous engineering efforts to reconstitute plant secondary metabolic pathways in microbial hosts (
6
,
9
–
13
), which almost always involve the functional reconstitution of plant CYPs, strategies to enhance CYP efficiency remain limited. The current approaches to engineer CYPs are generally focused on two major aspects: protein engineering of CYPs (e.g., protein evolution and N- or C-terminal engineering for localization) and electron transfer optimization (e.g., change pairing between CYP and CPR and tuning the expression of cytochrome
b5
[CYB5]), using alternative cofactors) (
8
). Although many of these strategies have successfully increased CYP performance in yeast, the results of the same strategies on different CYPs vary case by case. There have also been engineering efforts reported to increase the surface area of the ER membrane to enhance the efficiency of specific plant CYPs (
14
,
15
), but these also do not seem to be generally applicable.
Recently, Membrane Steroid-Binding Protein (MSBP) 1 from
Arabidopsis thaliana
(AtMSBP1) has been reported to function as a scaffold protein that supports the formation of the lignin biosynthetic complex by physically interacting with three monolignol biosynthetic CYPs (
16
). The ability of MSBP1 from
Saponaria vaccaria
to improve CYP efficiencies in baker’s yeast
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
was also recently reported in QS-21 biosynthesis (
17
). In this work, we investigated the effect of AtMSBP1 and its homologs in yeast strains engineered with diverse plant secondary metabolic pathways, including those for brassinosteroids (BRs), noscapine, and strigolactones (SLs), and observed broad enhancements in the functionality of CYPs involved in yeast. Beyond the prior hypothesis that MSBP1 regulates CYPs and thus enhances their production by scaffolding through interactions with CYPs and/or CPRs in yeast system (
16
,
17
), we find that interactions between AtMSBP1 and either CYP or CPR are not necessary for AtMSBP1 to enhance CYP functionality in yeast. Instead, AtMSBP1 facilitates CYP functionality through a much more sophisticated mechanism in yeast. Through coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) analysis, we found that AtMSBP1 recruits a much larger interactome in yeast when plant CYPs are expressed, compared to the wild-type yeast. Its interactome includes proteins mostly from the ER and some from mitochondria and vacuoles. In-depth exploration suggests that coexpression of AtMSBP1 with CYPs in yeast results in tubular ER expansion, mitochondrial volume increase, and vacuole fission, likely to enhance interorganelle communications. Our observations indicate that CYP reactions, although occurring at the ER membrane, involve more organelles and interorganelle communications than previously believed. This is further supported by the enhanced CYP efficiency when yeast proteins associated with these processes were overexpressed without AtMSBP1. This work highlights the importance of organelle coordination for CYP functionality in yeast, emphasizing the need to engineer the overall cellular microenvironment beyond just the ER and CYP themselves to establish yeast as a broadly adaptable host for producing plant secondary metabolites.
RESULTS
AtMSBP1 broadly enhances plant CYP performance in yeast
The fact that AtMSBP1 interacts with monolignol biosynthetic CYPs, forming a complex and stabilizing those CYPs (
16
), combined with its ability to bind to BRs and its negative role in BR signaling in plants (
18
), prompted us to hypothesize that AtMSBP1 may facilitate the function of CYPs in BR biosynthetic pathways. We previously constructed several phytosterol and BR-related biosynthetic yeast strains (
19
), including a campesterol-producing yeast strain YYL67 and a YYL69, which was based on YYL67 and expressed AtCYP90A1 and AtCYP90B1 (data S1). AtCYP90B1 catalyzes the C22-hydroxylation of campesterol, and AtCYP90A1 subsequently catalyzes C3-oxidation to form 22-OH-4-en-3-one (
Fig. 1A
). We introduced AtMSBP1 into YYL69 and observed an ~3-fold increase in 22-OH-4-en-3-one production per optical density at 600 nm (OD
600
) (
Fig. 1A
). In comparison, introducing AtMSBP1 to YYL67, a campesterol-producing strain without plant CYPs, increased the campesterol titer by only ~0.5-fold (fig. S1A). To test whether AtMSBP1 affects yeast indigenous ergosterol metabolism, where two CYPs are involved, we also introduced AtMSBP1 into wild-type yeast and did not observe any significant changes in ergosterol production (fig. S1A). This result indicates that, although AtMSBP1 influences plant sterol biosynthesis, it clearly has a more profound effect on the two CYPs involved in BR biosynthesis and has no impact on yeast indigenous ergosterol production (fig. S1B).

To further validate the role of AtMSBP1 in facilitating plant CYP activities in yeast, we examined its effect on another CYP from a sterol-independent pathway in yeast, 1-hydroxy-
N
-methylcanadine synthase (PsCYP82Y1), from the noscapine biosynthesis pathway in
Papaver somniferum
(
20
). PsCYP82Y1 catalyzes the conversion of
N
-methylcanadine to 1-hydroxy-
N
-methylcanadine (1-OH-methylcanadine), and
N
-methylcanadine is synthesized from canadine by tetrahydroprotoberberine
cis
-
N
-methyltransferase from
P. somniferum
(PsTNMT) (
20
) (
Fig. 1B
). Unlike the de novo phytosteroid biosynthesis in YYL69, where products remain within the cells, canadine was fed to yeast cultures, and its products were exported to and detected in the medium. Introducing AtMSBP1 into the yeast strain YYL143 (data S1), which expresses the cytochrome P450 reductase 1 from
A. thaliana
(ATR1), PsTNMT, and PsCYP82Y1 genes, resulted in an ~5-fold increase in 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine production per OD
600
(
Fig. 1B
), with the production of
N
-methylcanadine not affected by AtMSBP1 (fig. S2). Similar increases were also observed when AtMSBP1 was coexpressed with AcCYP722A from
Aquilegia coerulea
(~2-fold increase) or PpMAX1b from
Prunus persica
(~12-fold increase), two strigolactone-biosynthetic CYPs, in yeast (fig. S3 and data S1). Together with the recent reports showing the positive effects of AtMSBP1 or its paralogs on CYPs from other plant pathways in yeast (
17
,
21
,
22
), the positive impact of AtMSBP1 and its paralogs on plant CYPs, when heterologously expressed in yeast, appears to be generally applicable. Because of noticeable growth deficiencies caused by MSBPs (
Fig. 1
and figs. S1, S2, and S4), we estimated CYP performance in yeast by normalizing compound production to OD
600
.
To determine whether the CYP-supporting function of AtMSBP1 is unique or broadly conserved, we next examined its homologs across different species. AtMSBP1 belongs to the membrane-associated progesterone receptor (MAPR) subfamily, the members of which are broadly observed across eukaryotic organisms (
Fig. 1C
and fig. S5).
A. thaliana
encodes four MAPR proteins: AtMSBP1 (AT5G52240), AtMSBP2 (AT3G48890), AtMAPR2 (AT2G24940), and AtMAPR4 (AT4G14965).
S. cerevisiae
encodes one analog named damage response protein 1 (ScDAP1), which has been found to regulate the function of CYPs in yeast (
23
,
24
). In humans, two MAPR components (HsPGRMCs) have been identified, and they also are involved in many critical cellular processes, including regulating CYP functionality (
25
,
26
). In the phylogenetic analysis, most animals have two MAPRs and fungi only have one, whereas plants normally have more than three MAPRs (
Fig. 1C
, fig. S5, and data S2). The presence of more MAPR copies in plants likely reflects the greater complexity of plant metabolism compared to other eukaryotic organisms. Notably, the multiple copies of plant MAPRs also form a plant specific clade. This clade is divided into two subclades: AtMSBP1/2 belong to subclade I, which includes MAPRs widespread across land plants, whereas the smaller subclade II, including AtMAPR2, is found in only a few plant species (
Fig. 1C
).
To explore whether plant CYP-enhancing functionality is generally applicable among MAPR family proteins, we examined the four MAPR family proteins from
A. thaliana
, ScDAP1, HsPGRMC1, HsPGRMC2, and two more plant subclade I MAPRs, MpMSBP from
Marchantia polymorpha
, and OsMSBP from
Oryza sativa
. AtMSBP2 expression resulted in comparable increases to those seen with AtMSBP1 in YYL69 and YY143, 4- and 5-fold, respectively (
Fig. 1, A and B
). OsMSBP and MpMSBP exhibited similar levels of increases as AtMSBP1 in YYL143 (both ~4-fold) although lower in YYL69 (by ~1- and 2-fold, respectively). In contrast, ScDAP1 and HsPGRMCs also increased CYP efficiency in both YYL69 and YYL143 but only with half the enhancement of CYP efficiency compared to AtMSBP1/2. AtMAPR2 and AtMAPR4 did not increase CYP efficiency in YYL69 and YYL143, reflecting the diversity of MAPR proteins’ roles in plant (
Fig. 1, A and B
). MAPR proteins from diverse kingdoms enhance the conversion efficiency of CYP-catalyzed reactions, indicating a conserved role in supporting CYP functionality (
Fig. 1
). Among them, the plant MAPR subclade I exhibit the best performance in supporting plant CYP functionality in yeast, and AtMSBP1 was used for the following investigations.
AtMSBP1 supports CYP independently of CYB5, hemin, and interactions
Structure predictions of AtMSBP1 by AlphaFold (
27
) and TMHMM (
28
), combined with amino acid alignment analysis of MAPRs, reveal that AtMSBP1 can be divided into four domains: a lumen domain (A), a transmembrane domain (B), a CYB5-like domain (C), and an undefined disordered domain (D) (figs. S6 and S7A). Plant MAPR subclade I (AtMSBP1/2, OsMSBP, and MpMSBP) all share a similar structure. AtMAPR4 lacks the D domain. ScDAP1 and AtMAPR2 are unique, having only a C domain (fig. S6). Confocal microscopy imaging confirmed the lack of a transmembrane domain making ScDAP1 a cytosolic protein, whereas AtMSBP1 and HsPGRMC1 are localized at the ER membrane as previously reported (
25
) (fig. S7B). Notably, the C domain was highly conserved across MAPRs from all kingdoms (fig. S6). As heme binding is important for the function of CYB5, hemin, the oxidized form of heme, was fed to YYL69 and YYL143. Although hemin feeding increased CYP product levels in YYL69, it did not further enhance CYP efficiency when AtMSBP1 was present (fig. S8A). In YYL143, hemin supplementation showed no effect to CYP efficiency regardless of AtMSBP1 presence (fig. S8, A and B). Meanwhile, we overexpressed CYB5 from
S. cerevisiae
(ScCYB5) in YYL69 and YYL143 yet also did not observe the increased production of the corresponding products (fig. S8, C and D). Furthermore, we removed each of the four domains of AtMSBP1 and expressed them in YYL69 and YYL143 to explore the domain functions. Although the deletion of the C domain (AtMSBP1-ABD) significantly impaired AtMSBP1 function, the C domain alone (AtMSBP1-C) and the membrane-anchored C domain of AtMSBP1 (AtMSBP1-BC) nearly abolished the functions of AtMSBP1 in enhancing CYP functionality (fig. S7A). These results suggest that AtMSBP1 does not play the same role as CYB5, and its function in supporting CYPs is likely heme independent.
Notably, the deletion of the unique disordered D domain of plant MAPR subclade I led to a significant decrease in AtMSBP1’s ability to support CYP functionality (AtMSBP1 versus AtMSBP1-ABC, AtMSBP1-BCD versus AtMSBP1-BC, and AtMSBP1-CD versus AtMSBP1-C; fig. S7A), suggesting a critical role of this domain. The deletion of D domain also led to a lower expression level of AtMSBP1, indicating that this domain might be important for AtMSBP1 folding and stability (fig. S7C). These results imply that the plant MAPR subclade I with its unique structure represents a distinct subgroup specialized in enhancing plant CYP performance in yeast.
In addition, a previous study suggests that plant subclade I MAPRs may enhance CYP functionality through providing a scaffold to form a complex and stabilize CYPs (
17
). To investigate whether protein-protein interactions also contribute to the enhancement of plant CYP efficiency in yeast, we used a mating-based split-ubiquitin yeast two-hybrid (mbSUS-Y2H) system (
29
) to examine the physical interactions between MAPRs and AtCYP90A1, PsCYP82Y1, or ATR1 (
Fig. 1D
). AtCYP90B1 was excluded due to background growth in the mbSUS-Y2H system (see details in Materials and Methods). Interactions of MAPR proteins, except for AtMAPR4, with AtCYP90A1 were observed but not with PsCYP82Y1 (
Fig. 1D
). Interactions between all MAPRs and ATR1 were not detected (
Fig. 1D
). Meanwhile, ATR1 interacts with AtCYP90A1 but not with PsCYP82Y1 (
Fig. 1D
). Furthermore, the interactions between AtMSBP1 reconfigured mutants and AtCYP90A1 were examined (fig. S7D). All mutants, including the least active variant AtMSBP1-BC, retained, although weakened, the interaction with AtCYP90A1. This suggests that the physical interaction of MAPRs with CYPs or CPR is not strictly required for enhancing CYP functionality in yeast. Thus, MAPRs are likely to promote CYP functionality through a more complex mechanism beyond simple scaffolding in yeast.
AtMSBP1 interactome enriched by plant CYP expression in yeast
Given that MAPRs show no catalytic activity but interact with a diversity of proteins (
16
,
18
) (
Fig. 1D
), analyzing their interactome in yeast may provide insights into how MAPRs enhance CYP functionality in yeast. Immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry (IP-MS) analysis (
30

Non-ER mechanisms essential for AtMSBP1 enhance CYP functionality in yeast
To identify proteins that assist AtMSBP1 in enhancing plant CYP functionality in yeast, 17 gene candidates from each subcluster were selected, excluding those related to ribosomes or redundant functions (table S2). Attempts to inactivate these genes in YYL69 and wild-type yeast often impaired growth or induced apoptosis, particularly in YYL69. Therefore, we assessed their impact by overexpressing the candidates in two different CYP-expressing strains, YYL69 and YYL143 (data S1), with and without AtMSBP1 (
Fig. 2E
and figs. S9 and S10). Proteins that increased CYP performance only when coexpressed with AtMSBP1, but showed no significant change without it, are likely involved in AtMSBP1’s role in enhancing CYP functionality.
When AtMSBP1 was present, overexpression of RTN1, VMA2, and AFG1 led to a significant increase in the production of 22-OH-4-en-3-one catalyzed by AtCYP90A1 and AtCYP90B1 from campesterol in YYL69 and 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine catalyzed by PsCYP82Y1 from
N

Fig. 2E
and figs. S9 and S10). Furthermore, remaining untested proteins (TCB3, VMA4, VMA13, MGR3, and PHB1) in the clusters containing RTN1, VMA2, or AFG1, excluding ribosome-related proteins, were assessed in YYL69 and YYL143. MGR3 and PHB1, from the AFG1 cluster, enhanced CYP performances in both strains in the presence of AtMSBP1 (
Fig. 2E
and figs. S9 and S10). Overall, five candidates (RTN1, VMA2, AFG1, MRG3, and PHB1) are most likely involved in AtMSBP1’s role in supporting plant CYP functionality.
RTN1 is a reticulon protein involved in tubular area formation of the ER membrane (
34

35

36

37

38

The direct interactions between the five candidates and AtMSBP1 were evaluated using the mbSUS-Y2H assay or bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), showing AtMSBP1 has a direct interaction with RTN1 and VMA2 but not with PHB1, MRG3, or AFG1 (fig. Among them, only RTN1 showed an interaction with AtCYP90A1, whereas none interacted with PsCYP82Y1 (fig. S11C). These results suggest that the five candidates are more likely involved in AtMSBP1-mediated mechanisms, rather than only interacting with plant CYPs in yeast.
Of the five candidates, AFG1, PHB1, and MGR3 are all mitochondrial proteins. This raises questions about AtMSBP1’s potential association with mitochondria. To address this, AtMSBP1-DsRed was expressed in yeast alongside a mitochondrial membrane marker, COX15-EGFP. The confocal images confirmed that AtMSBP1-DsRed did not overlap with mitochondria (fig. S12), suggesting that AtMSBP1 is associated with mitochondrial proteins indirectly.
AtMSBP1 improves ER membrane distribution in yeast
The ER membrane is an essential eukaryotic organelle where proteins and lipids are synthesized (
41
). It is mainly composed of three domains: the nuclear envelope, the sheetlike cisternae, and the tubular network (
41
). RTN1 is a reticulon protein that is important for the morphology of the tubular ER, where communications between the ER and the other organelles (such as mitochondria and Golgi) occur. RTN1 was also highly enriched in AtMSBP1’s interactome in YYL69 (
Fig. 2C
and data S1). Hence, investigating the distribution of RTN1 and the morphology of the ER membrane, particularly the tubular region, could provide insights into how ER-localized AtMSBP1 recruits proteins from the other organelles. The EGFP was thus fused to the C terminus of RTN1 and expressed in YYL143 (data S1) and wild-type yeast, with or without AtMSBP1. YYL69 was not used for confocal microscopy imaging due to its deteriorated growth and smaller cell size. Both the center section of cells and stacked three-dimensional (3D) images showed that coexpression of AtMSBP1 in YYL143 led to a much more extensive tubular ER network, compared to YYL143 alone (
Fig. 3A
). Noticeably, RTN1-EGFP was more evenly distributed in YYL143 with AtMSBP1 as fewer condensed RTN1-EGFP spots were observed (
Fig. 3A
and data S4). In addition, RTN1-EGFP intensity per cell was significantly lower in AtMSBP1-expressing YYL143 than in YYL143 alone, likely due to the ability to properly distribute RTN1-EGFP within the larger tubular ER (fig. S13A). Similar tubular ER extension was observed with ScDAP1 and HsPGRMC1 overexpression in YYL143 but not with the inactive AtMSBP1-BC variant (fig. S13B), suggesting a correlation between tubular ER extension and improved CYP functionality in yeast. However, the expression of AtMSBP1 in wild-type yeast did not cause such changes (
Fig. 3A
and fig. S13A), indicating that AtMSBP1 plays a role in modulating the distribution of RTN1 only when plant CYPs are present. Corresponding quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed no significant changes in
RTN1
transcript level in YYL143 and wild-type yeast when AtMSBP1 was expressed, except a slight increase in YYL69 (
P
value = 0.039; fig. S13C), suggesting that AtMSBP1 likely modulates tubular ER morphology at the protein level, rather than gene transcription level.

AtMSBP1 enhances mitochondrial volume in yeast
Mitochondria generate most of the chemical energy needed for cellular biochemical reactions (
42
). Their dynamic structure, maintained by fission (regulated by DNM1) and fusion (regulated by FZO1), is essential for proper mitochondrial function (
43
). As three AtMSPB1’s interactors (AFG1, MGR3, and PHB1) are mitochondrial proteins, we monitored the mitochondrial morphology using COX15-EGFP as a marker in YYL143 and wild-type yeast, with and without AtMSBP1 (data S1). Because mitochondrial dynamics change during cell growth, and aging increases mitochondrial fission (
44
), we examined CYP efficiency over time. PsCYP82Y1 efficiency dropped markedly after 24 hours of cultivation in YYL143 (fig. S14). Therefore, we collected confocal images of mitochondria at 6, 12, and 18 hours postinoculation to represent the active status and at 24 hours to represent the inactive status for comparison. Confocal imaging revealed no significant differences between 6-hour samples of YYL143 (
Fig. 3, B and C
, and data S4) and the wild type (fig. S15, A and B, and data S4), regardless of AtMSBP1 expression. However, mitochondrial volumes in YYL143 decreased significantly at 12 hours and remained low thereafter (
Fig. 3, B and C
). In contrast, AtMSBP1 expression in YYL143 increased mitochondrial volume after 12 hours, maintaining elevated levels over time (
Fig. 3, B and C
). Consequently, mitochondrial volumes in AtMSBP1-expressing YYL143 were significantly higher than in YYL143 alone (
Fig. 3, B and C
). In addition, the inactive AtMSBP1-BC had a very minimal effect on mitochondrial volume (fig. S15C). Notably, overexpressing HsPGRMC1 and ScDAP1, which also enhances CYP functionality but to a lesser extent than AtMSBP1, has different effects on mitochondrial volume. HsPGRMC1 overexpression increased mitochondrial volume, albeit to a lower degree than AtMSBP1 expression, whereas ScDAP1 overexpression did not affect mitochondrial volume (fig. S15C). These results suggest that increased mitochondrial volume may contribute to enhanced CYP functionality; however, enhanced CYP performance does not necessarily require a corresponding increase in mitochondrial volume. Wild-type yeast cells, nevertheless, maintain consistent mitochondrial volumes regardless of AtMSBP1 expression, except for the 18-hour incubation time (fig. S15, A and B, and data S4). In addition, the decrease in mitochondrial volumes of YYL143 compared to wild-type yeast also suggested potential redox stress elicited by the presence of heterologous plant CYPs in yeast (
Fig. 3C
and fig. S15B).
To explore how AtMSBP1 affects mitochondrial volume, we examined the effect of AtMSBP1 on fusion and fission, the two major elements that control mitochondria dynamics (
43
). The transcription levels of the fusion-related gene
FZO1
and the fission-related gene
DNM1
were quantified by qRT-PCR (fig. S15, D and E). AtMSBP1 expressions significantly increased
FZO1
transcription in YYL143 and YYL69 (fig. S15D) but did not result in a significant change of
DNM1
transcription (fig. S15E). In contrast, AtMSBP1 expression drastically decreased the transcription of both genes in wild-type yeast (fig. S15, D and E). This observation, along with the finding that increased mitochondrial volume only occurred when AtMSBP1 was expressed in the presence of plant CYPs, suggests that AtMSBP1’s role in regulating mitochondria is activated specifically when plant CYPs are present and likely preferentially through regulating FZO1 expression.
To determine whether altered fission and fusion of mitochondria are related to CYP functionality, we overexpressed FZO1 and DNM1 in YYL69 and YYL143. FZO1 overexpression increased the production of 22-OH-4-en-3-one and 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine by ~2-fold in YYL69 and 4-fold in YYL143 (fig. S16, A and B) although with a negative impact on growth. DNM1 overexpression also reduced growth but had minimal impacts on production per cell (fig. S16, A and B). Coexpression of FZO1 and DNM1 did not enhance CYP performance as effectively as FZO1 alone (fig. S16, A and B). Microscopy analysis showed that FZO1 overexpression did not promote fusion or increase mitochondrial volume (fig. S16C). Instead, it induced mitochondria fragmentation or aggregation, suggesting a more complex mitochondria regulation in yeast, as previously reported (
45
) (fig. S16D).
In addition, we quantified the total NADPH/NADP levels in YYL143 with and without AtMSBP1, using the inactive AtMSBP1-BC variant as a control, after 12 hours of cultivation, when the mitochondrial volume differences became evident (fig. S16E). No significant changes in NADPH/NADP levels were observed, suggesting that AtMSBP1 did not enhance CYP functionality by altering the total NADPH/NADP supply. Overall, the increased mitochondrial volume in YYL143 expressing AtMSBP1 likely contributes to enhanced CYP functionality, although it is not the sole reason, and FZO1 appears to play an essential and complex role in this process.
AtMSBP1 enhances vacuole fission in yeast
The enrichment of VMA2, a subunit of vacuolar H
+
-ATPase, when AtMSBP1 was coexpressed with CYPs, raises the question of whether vacuoles are also involved in AtMSBP1’s role in supporting CYP functionality. To investigate this, we monitored vacuole morphology using VAC8-EGFP (
46
) in YYL143 and wild-type yeast (data S1), with and without AtMSBP1. Morphology was analyzed at 12 and 24 hours, corresponding to active and inactive CYP states. Wild-type yeast and YYL143 showed comparable vacuole morphology, with most cells containing three to eight vacuoles (
Fig. 3D
), indicating that plant CYP expression has little impact on vacuole dynamics. AtMSBP1 had minimal impact on vacuole dynamics in wild-type yeast (
Fig. 3D
) but increased vacuole fission in YYL143, resulting in smaller, fragmented vesicles regardless of cell age (
Fig. 3D
and fig. S17). The inactive mutant AtMSBP1-BC did not affect vacuole morphology in YYL143 (fig. S17), suggesting that AtMSBP1’s ability to support CYP functionality is related to its role in promoting vacuole fission. Increased vacuole fission may indicate higher cellular stress and an elevated demand for microautophagy (
47
,
48
). Studies on aging and vacuole morphology suggest that increased vacuole fission shortens cellular life span (
49
). Consistently, we observed a reduced life span in YYL143 cells expressing AtMSBP1 compared to those without, suggesting that coexpression of AtMSBP1 with plant CYPs may exaggerate cell stress. We therefore speculate that vacuole fission may help cells function more efficiently under metabolically demanding and stressful conditions by increasing vacuolar surface area and volume.
AtMSBP1-independent engineering equally enhances plant CYP performance in yeast
Given the intriguing correlation between the morphological change of subcellular organelles (ER, vacuole, and mitochondria) and CYP functionality, we investigated whether these morphological changes could directly enhance CYP performance. Because AtMSBP1 overexpression induces such morphological alterations and likely functions by coordinating interactions among proteins localized at different organelles (
Fig. 2
), we hypothesize that its interactome components may shape this microenvironment. To test this, we overexpressed AtMSBP1 interactors (RTN1, VMA2, AFG1, MGR3, and PHB1) in different combinations (
Fig. 4A
). Among the 18 combinations tested in YYL143, overexpression of RTN1/AFG1/MGR3 and RTN1/AFG1/VMA2 led to greater enhancement of CYP efficiency compared to AtMSBP1 alone (
Fig. 4A
). Notably, further coexpressing AtMSBP1 with RTN1/AFG1/MGR3 only resulted in a slight increase in 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine production (
Fig. 4A
), suggesting that their roles on supporting CYP functionality might be redundant. A similar trend was observed in YYL69, although with lower fold change, likely due to the strain-specific severe growth deficiencies (fig. S18). Confocal imaging of YYL143 overexpressing RTN1/AFG1/MGR3 and RTN1/AFG1/VMA2 revealed enhanced mitochondrial volume, expanded tubular ER, more evenly distributed RTN1, and enhanced vacuole fission (
Fig. 4B
and fig. S19), consistent with the effects observed in YYL143 expressing AtMSBP1. Although the exact role of AFG1 and VMA2, as ATPases, in driving these morphological changes remains unclear, the consistent organelle remodeling and the comparable impact on CYP performance imply the importance of mitochondria expansion, tubular ER extension, and vacuole fission in supporting CYP functionality. This also emphasizes the need for in-depth cellular and biochemical studies for achieving precise metabolic or cellular engineering, even in well-characterized model organisms like baker’s yeast.

Interorganelle communications are essential for CYP functionality
The desired morphological change that supports CYP functionality all appears to improve interorganelle contact and interactions. In addition, the ER has been found to function as a platform for communication and exchange of materials between organelles (
41
). This prompted us to investigate whether cross-organelle coordination and interactions are essential for CYP functionality.
Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), the connections between mitochondria and the ER membrane, are critical for mitochondria dynamics and play an essential role in subcellular functions such as calcium ion homeostasis, lipid transfer, signaling, and apoptosis (
50
). In yeast, MAMs are typically tethered by a complex comprising MMM1, MDM10, MDM12, and MDM34 (
51
). MMM1 is an ER-anchored protein, MDM12 is a cytoplasmic junction protein, and MDM34 and MDM10 are outer mitochondrial membrane proteins (
51
). MAM dynamics were assessed in different strains with CYPs and/or AtMSBP1, by monitoring the expression and localization of MMM1-EGFP fusion protein (data S1). No significant differences were observed across the strains or conditions tested (fig. S20, A and B). Meanwhile, attempts to quantify the overlapping area of the ER and mitochondria using confocal microscopy were unsuccessful due to the low rendering quality of the complex ER membrane, making it impossible to generate reliable results. Without a valid method to quantify MAM interaction areas, we measured the transcript levels of
MMM1
and
MDM12
, two key subunits of the MAM tethering complex, using qRT-PCR in YYL69, YYL143, and wild-type yeast, with and without the expression of AtMSBP1. AtMSBP1 expression increased
MMM1
transcript levels in YYL69 and YYL143 but not in the wild type (fig. S21A). In comparison, the expression of AtMSBP1 did not affect the cytosolic component MDM12 across all strains tested (fig. S21B).
In addition, we used mbSUS-Y2H to examine the interactions between MMM1, MDM12, and MAPRs. Cytosolic MDM12 resulted in false positives, and the results were not valid. MMM1 strongly interacted with MAPRs from subclade I (AtMSBP1, AtMSBP2, OsMSBP, and MpMSBP), weakly with AtMAPR2, HsPGRMC1, and ScDAP1, and showed no interaction with AtMAPR4 (fig. S21D). These interactions aligned with the ability of MAPRs to enhance CYP functionality, suggesting that the plant MAPR subclade I’s CYP-enhancing function may be related to MAM regulation. Furthermore, overexpression of MMM1 in YYL69 and YYL143 significantly increased CYP efficiency, despite severely impaired yeast growth (
Fig. 4A
and fig. S18).
LTC1 is the lipid transfer protein located at the contact sites of ER-vacuole, ER-mitochondria, and vacuole-mitochondria (
52
,
53
). Previous research showed that LTC1 overexpression enhances interorganelle associations between ER, mitochondria, and vacuoles (
52
). Consistent with our observation of MMM1, overexpression of LTC1 enhanced 22-OH-4-en-3-one production by 1.6-fold in YYL69 and 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine by 4-fold in YYL143, compared to the empty vector control (
Fig. 4A
and fig. S18). As expected, LTC1 overexpression in YYL143 led to the extended tubular ER, enhanced mitochondrial volume (mainly enhanced fusion, not as high as AtMSBP1), and increased vacuole fission, aligning with the effects observed with AtMSBP1 expression (
Fig. 4B
and data S4). qRT-PCR analysis revealed that AtMSBP1 expression increased
LTC1
transcription in YYL69 but not in YYL143 or the wild type, indicating that AtMSBP1 is not directly involved in
LTC1
transcription regulation (fig. S21C). Minimal interactions were observed between LTC1 and MAPRs (fig. S21E), consistent with the absence of LTC1 in AtMSBP1 interactomes (
Fig. 2D
), suggesting that AtMSBP1 does not function through LTC1. Furthermore, coexpression of LTC1 and AtMSBP1 enhanced 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine production by 11-fold in YYL143 (
Fig. 4A
) and 22-OH-4-en-3-one by 5-fold in YYL69 (fig. S18), outperforming individual LTC1 or AtMSBP1 overexpression. The overexpression of RTN1/AFG1/MGR3 with LTC1 further enhanced the production of 1-OH-
N
-methylcanadine by ~19-fold in YYL143, highlighting the power of coordinating interorganelle communication in boosting CYP efficiency. Together, optimizing cross-organelle coordination, rather than focusing solely on ER modification or CYP/CPR paring and engineering, represents a promising and more broadly applicable strategy to enhance plant CYP functionality in yeast.
DISCUSSION
Engineering yeast for plant natural product biosynthesis has been an important research focus for decades. Traditional strategies primarily focus on protein and pathway engineering. This study highlights an alternative strategy using a universal “enhancer” scaffold protein, AtMSBP1, to improve plant CYP functionality in baker’s yeast. By examining how AtMSBP1 enhances CYP functionality, we explored the cellular mechanisms regulating CYP performance in yeast. Through an extensive interactome analysis of AtMSBP1 in yeast expressing plant CYPs, we revealed that plant CYP functionality involves multiple organelles beyond simply the ER membrane, with mitochondria playing a particularly critical role, which was not previously reported (
Fig. 4C
). By adjusting the expression levels of just four endogenous genes that regulate organelle morphology and interactions, plant CYP efficiency was enhanced by more than 19-fold in yeast. Beyond providing practical guidance for engineering a microenvironment supporting CYP functionality, our study also emphasizes the potential of yeast as a versatile cell factory to carry plant biosynthetic machinery. These findings extend our understanding of yeast engineering for plant CYPs and highlight organelle coordination as a promising strategy for future metabolic engineering efforts.
Given that type II CYPs are localized to the ER and rely on electron transfer from reducing partners and supply of NADPH (primarily supplied by mitochondria) for activity, the need for efficient enzyme-organelle and interorganelle communication is well justified. It is therefore reasonable to hypothesize that enhanced interorganelle connectivity, potentially driven by MAPR-induced morphological changes, contributes to improved CYP performance. If so, the function of MAPRs and the strategies developed here by studying AtMSBP1 may not be limited to plant CYPs but could extend to type II CYPs broadly. To test this, we examined HsCYP17A1 from
Homo sapiens
, which catalyzes the conversion from progesterone to 17α-OH-progesterone. As expected, coexpression with MAPRs like HsPGRMC1/2 or AtMSBP1/2 increased 17α-OH-progesterone production. Notably, overexpression of LTC1, RTN1/AFG1, and RTN1/AFG1/VMA2 also led to significant enhancement in the production of 17α-OH-progesterone (fig. S22). These results highlight the broad applicability of MAPRs and the strategies developed in this study for enhancing functionality of type II CYPs across diverse species. It is widely accepted that providing the correct microenvironment is essential for heterologous proteins to function correctly ex situ or in vitro. A recent report has indicated that membrane-anchored CYPs and CPRs tend to selectively associate with specific phospholipids through protein-lipid interactions (
54
). The heterogeneity of membrane lipids could result in colocalization or separation of CYPs and CPRs, which, in turn, affect the CYP functionality (
54
). Similarly, our previous work also showed that the sterol composition of membranes could affect CYP performance (
55
). Specifically, we found that plant CYP activity is higher in phytosterol-producing yeast strains, compared to wild-type yeast, which produces ergosterol (
55
). However, these prior engineering efforts have yielded limited success and were not as effective. Our findings resolve this limitation by revealing the critical role of interorganelle interactions, emphasizing the need to precisely modulate organelle morphology and interactions to create an optimal intracellular environment for CYP functionality. Nevertheless, fundamental gaps remain in our understanding of organelle regulation. For example, vacuole fission is proved to be related to AtMSBP1-mediated enhancement of plant CYP functionality, but its mechanistic role remains unclear. It is uncertain whether vacuole fission is a consequence of elevated cellular activity driven by increased CYP demand or whether the fission process itself actively contributes to improved CYP functionality. Such knowledge gaps emphasize the urgent need for in-depth mechanistic studies in yeast to enable precise tailoring of cellular microenvironments for specialized enzyme functions, such as plant CYPs.
In addition, the AtMSBP1 domain reconfiguration experiments revealed a context-dependent mechanism of AtMSBP1 regulating protein interactions. The deletion of a transmembrane domain (B) or disordered domain (D) weakened its interaction with AtCYP90A1 (fig. S7D) and brassinosteroid insensitive 1-associated receptor kinase 1 (BAK1), a kinase reported to interact with AtMSBP1 in BR signaling (
18
) (fig. S23A). On the other hand, the cytosolic mutant, AtMSBP1-CD, completely abolished the interaction with BAK1 yet retained the interaction with AtCYP90A1 (fig. S7D). Notably, whereas the full-length AtMSBP1 showed no interaction with PsCYP82Y1, the deletion of A domain (AtMSBP1-BCD) resulted in a very weak interaction (fig. S23B). These differential interaction profiles suggest AtMSBP1 as a multifunctional scaffold using distinct domains to regulate different biological processes through selective partner recognition.
In this study, we explored only one aspect of AtMSBP1’s function: its role in supporting CYP functionality in a heterologous host,
S. cerevisiae
. However, its native regulatory mechanisms in plants are likely much more intricate. Beyond its involvement in plant secondary metabolism via CYP regulation, AtMSBP1 has been shown to play a role in BR signaling (
18
,
56
), plant photomorphogenesis (
57
), formation of arbuscular mycorrhiza (
56
), autophagy (
58
), and many more. Our findings, alongside previous works, suggest that plant MAPR subclade I may play a central role in regulating plant metabolism. Plant MAPRs are clearly a protein family worthy of further in-depth investigation, for a better understanding into how plants regulate biosynthesis and signaling, and ultimately promoting our capability to engineer plant metabolic networks to address global challenges including but not limited to food security and climate change.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
General culture conditions
Yeast strains were cultured in 30°C in a complex yeast extract, peptone, and dextrose (YPD; all components from BD Diagnostics) medium or synthetic defined medium (SDM) containing yeast nitrogen base (YNB) (BD Diagnostics), ammonium sulfate (Fisher Scientific), 2% (w/v) glucose, unless specified, and the appropriate dropout (Takara Bio) solution for selection.
For metabolite analysis, yeast strains were first cultured overnight in 500 μl of SDM with 2% (w/v) glucose in 96-well plates (BD Falcon) at 30°C overnight, at 250 rpm. The appropriate volume of the overnight seed culture was inoculated in fresh 500-μl SDM with glucose to make the OD
600
around 0.1 and incubated at 30°C for 72 hours before metabolite analysis of the yeast pellets or medium. The OD
600
of the culture was measured by a Molecular Devices QuickDrop Spectrophotometer.
General technique for DNA manipulation
PCR reactions were performed with an Expand High Fidelity system (Sigma-Aldrich), Phusion DNA Polymerase (NEB), Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (New England Biolabs), or Taq Polymerase (NEB) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. PCR products were purified by the Zymoclean Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research). Plasmids were prepared with EconoSpin columns (Epoch Life Science) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. The labeling reaction was terminated by addition of 0.9 μl of quenching solution (5% hydroxylamine in 50 mM Hepes (pH 8.5)] and vortexing at RT for 15 min. LC-MS and MS/MS analyses were conducted on a Fusion Lumos Orbitrap tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with an Easy 1000 nLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a Flex nanoelectrospray ion source (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The mass spectrometer was equipped with a high-field asymmetric-waveform ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS), where the compensation voltages (CVs) were set at −40, −60, and −80 V. The mbSUS-Y2H system to detect protein-protein interaction
For the Y2H assay, we followed a standard protocol for the mbSUS-Y2H system. Briefly, the encoding genes of proteins to be detected were cloned to pDonor221 (Invitrogen) without stop codons. Those genes were then used with Gateway LR Clonase II to clone into the pMetYC-DEST vector to generate the bait constructs with Cub fused to the C termini of encoding genes or into the pXN22-DEST vector to generate prey constructs with Nub fused to the C termini of encoding genes (data S1). The bait and prey constructs were transformed into CD3-808 and CD3-809 yeast strains and selected on –Leu and –Trp/–Ura plates, respectively. By mating, the diploid cells harboring both constructs were selected on –Trp, –Leu, and –Ura plates. Positive cells were serially diluted and plated on the six selective medium –Trp, –Leu, –Ade, –His, –Ura, and –Met. Images were taken after 3 to 5 days of growth. In the mbSUS-Y2H system, bait and prey proteins are separately fused with N terminus (Nub) and C terminus (Cub) of a ubiquitin. Because MAPR proteins, AtCYP90B1 and RTN1, VMA2 fused with Cub always result in background growth, we can only test the interactions of MAPR-Nub with AtCYP90A1-Cub and PsCYP82Y1-Cub. The interaction between AtMSBP1 and RTN1, VMA2, was validated through BiFC.
